With the launch of the M6 Mac mini and its beefed-up M5 Pro sibling, Apple has quietly killed one of the machine's most appealing features. While the two new Mac minis look similar to the previous generation on the outside, the company has removed a hidden feature that made the last Mac mini a tremendous value.

When the M4 Mac mini debuted, it was already a tremendous value. It packed Apple's M4 SoC, a generous 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. Starting at $599 (or $499 for students), the M4 Mac mini wasn't just the most versatile Mac in Apple's lineup — it was the best Mac you could get at its price.

Video: Apple killed the Mac mini's most useful hidden feature :(

However, this smallest Mac of Apple's had an unreleased feature that made it even more of a value — an upgradable storage slot. By prying off the bottom cover and removing a few screws, users could access a removable NAND module and swap in a third-party SSD for up to 2TB of additional storage.

The benefits didn't end there. Users could upgrade their SSDs or easily replace a failed drive, and they could save money by avoiding Apple's custom upgrade options in favor of cheaper third-party SSDs.

Apple's own 2TB upgrade cost $400, turning a "cheap" computer into a $1400 one with the click of a button. By purchasing and installing a third-party SSD later, users could save nearly $500.

Of course, as a self-proclaimed DIY enthusiast, I was thrilled by this and even produced a full video tutorial walking through how to upgrade the stock SSD to a third-party drive. The response was very enthusiastic, with the video racking up 500,000 views.

Video: How to upgrade M4 Mac mini SSD

Those good times didn't last.

With the latest generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly to the logic board, completely removing the possibility for users to upgrade to a third-party NAND module after purchase.

What was once arguably the best value Mac has become a much more expensive product, with the base model jumping from $600 to $900 and the 2TB upgrade increasing from $800 to $1000.

If you want to buy an M6 Mac mini with 2TB of storage today, it will cost you $1900 from Apple. With the equivalent M4 Mac mini and a 2TB aftermarket upgrade, the total cost was around $920, including a $320 aftermarket upgrade. Of course, prices have gone up across the board since then, so it's not entirely apples to apples, but we're talking about a $1000 price increase that isn't just Apple charging more. It's Apple removing the ability to upgrade.

I can probably guess why Apple raised the price of the base model Mac mini by $300, and even why the SSD prices have gone up so dramatically. Prices for components, SSDs, and memory have all gone up significantly due to factors including AI. That doesn't explain why Apple chose to solder the SSD to the logic board rather than keeping the user-replaceable design.

We can speculate, but the real reason behind Apple's decision may never be public. What we do know is that the price of these machines has skyrocketed, and "skyrocketed" might be an understatement. Comparing the M4 Mac mini with a 2TB aftermarket upgrade to the M6 Mac mini with a 2TB custom upgrade, the price has gone up by approximately 106%.

9to5Mac's Take

Finding a base model M4 Mac mini on the used market at a reasonable price might be difficult, but if you can, its base performance, features, and upgradeable SSD make it still a phenomenal machine.

The good news is that all Mac mini models feature Thunderbolt, so you can easily add high-bandwidth storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. I'm personally a big fan of the Samsung T9 as a relatively affordable way to add more storage.

What do you think Apple's reasoning is for removing user-replaceable storage from the Mac mini? Have any specific theories? Let us know in the comments.
